newsitem.title: THAILAND: Thai shrimp industry hit by trade barriers, costs.
newsitem.headline: Thai shrimp industry hit by trade barriers, costs.

text.p: Thailand's multi-billion-dollar shrimp industry has been hit hard by Western trade barriers, higher production costs and disease, officials and industry sources said.
Although Thailand still dominates the major world frozen shrimp markets, all signs point to its share declining in the future, the sources told Reuters.

Thai frozen shrimp exports to the key Japanese and U.S. markets fell 24.51 percent in the first seven months of 1996 from the same period last year, says a report by agri-business giant Charoen Pokphand (CP), the largest shrimp exporter.

During that time, shrimp exports by regional competitors Indonesia, India and Bangladesh, whose prices are cheaper because of lower production costs, rose in those two markets by 4.30 percent, 4.79 percent and 46.23 percent.

"Especially in Japan, an economic slowdown and the yen depreciation make imported shrimps unattractive," a CP official said, adding that Japan's shrimp imports were down this year. Competition could be even tougher for Thailand next year.
Beginning in January, Thai frozen shrimp no longer will qualify for the special tariff privileges the European Union gives developing nations, a Commerce Ministry official said.
"This means Thai frozen shrimp will face higher import tariffs than those from competitors such as India and Indonesia by at least five percent," the CP official said.
Also, U.S. environmental concerns and the outbreak of disease in shrimp have hurt the local shrimp farming industry.
The U.S. Court of International Trade in October 1995 barred the import of shrimp caught at sea by ships not using devices or techniques to protect sea turtles, an endangered species.
The U.S. government followed last May 1 with a ban on Thai shrimp. The State Department lifted the embargo last Friday after Thailand complied with the American regulations.

Only 10 per cent of Thailand's output are sea shrimp, but the industry had feared the U.S. ban would mean more shrimp dumped onto the local market and lower domestic prices. The situation was expected to be improve with the ending of the ban.
Thailand exported shrimp worth about $550 million to the United States in 1995.
Meanwhile, the local supply of shrimp has dropped because of disease among the virus-prone shellfish, especially in the densely farmed south of Thailand.
"The situation is improving now and we have been given technical solutions to the problem by the government. But it could reoccur," said a Bangkok-based operator of a shrimp farm in the south.
Industry sources said the shrimp supply this year was expected to drop 6.6 percent from last year to 210,000 tonnes.
However, The CP report said the outlook for shrimp exports would improve if Thailand develops new markets in China, South Korea and Taiwan.
